sections.title: Galvanic cells: chemistry into current

board_events.text: Galvanic cell: spontaneous redox → electricity
Two tanks joined by a pipe: water flows high to low until levels match.
Here the "water" is electrons and the "height" is electrical potential.
Anode (left): oxidation, Zn dissolves. Cathode (right): reduction, Cu plates out.
In a galvanic cell the anode is $-$ and the cathode is $+$.

board_events.text: Electrons flow anode $\rightarrow$ cathode in the wire; conventional current the opposite way.

segments.text: Let's start with a picture. Two water tanks on a roof joined by a pipe: water rushes from the higher tank to the lower until the levels equalise, and then flow stops.
An electrochemical cell is exactly that image, except the water is electrons and the height difference is electrical potential.
A galvanic cell lets a spontaneous redox reaction push those electrons through an external wire, turning chemical energy into electrical energy.
The classic example is the Daniell cell. Here is its overall reaction: solid zinc plus copper ions give zinc ions plus solid copper.

Zinc is more eager to give up electrons, so at the zinc electrode zinc atoms dissolve, leaving electrons behind. That is oxidation, and this electrode is the anode. At the copper electrode, copper ions grab electrons and plate out as metal. That is reduction, at the cathode.

<curious>Now here is a sign convention worth burning in.</curious> In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and the cathode is positive. Later, in electrolysis, these flip, so lock the galvanic version in now.

Look at the setup: a zinc rod in zinc sulphate on the left, a copper rod in copper sulphate on the right, a wire through a voltmeter reading about one point one zero volts, and an inverted salt bridge joining the beakers.
The electrons released at the anode travel through the wire to the cathode. Conventional current, the old positive-charge direction, runs the opposite way, from cathode to anode.
एक picture से शुरू करते हैं। छत पर दो water tanks एक pipe से जुड़े हैं: पानी ऊँचे tank से नीचे वाले में तब तक बहता है जब तक levels बराबर न हो जाएँ, फिर flow रुक जाता है।
एक electrochemical cell बिल्कुल यही image है, बस यहाँ पानी की जगह electrons हैं और height की जगह electrical potential।
Galvanic cell एक spontaneous redox reaction को external wire से electrons push करने देता है, यानी chemical energy को electrical energy में बदल देता है।
Classic example है Daniell cell। यह रही इसकी overall reaction: solid zinc और copper ions मिलकर zinc ions और solid copper देते हैं।

Zinc electrons देने में ज़्यादा eager है, तो zinc electrode पर zinc atoms घुल जाते हैं और electrons पीछे छोड़ देते हैं — यह oxidation है, और यह electrode anode है। Copper electrode पर copper ions electrons पकड़ कर metal की तरह plate out हो जाते हैं — यह reduction, cathode पर।
<curious>अब एक sign convention पक्का याद रखो।</curious> Galvanic cell में anode negative होता है और cathode positive। आगे electrolysis में ये उल्टे हो जाते हैं, तो galvanic वाला अभी lock कर लो।

Setup देखो: left पर zinc rod, zinc sulphate में; right पर copper rod, copper sulphate में; एक wire जिसमें voltmeter करीब one point one zero volts दिखा रहा है; और एक inverted salt bridge दोनों beakers को जोड़ रहा है।
Anode पर निकले electrons wire से cathode तक जाते हैं। Conventional current, positive charge की पुरानी direction, उल्टी चलती है — cathode से anode की ओर।

sections.title: The salt bridge: the quiet circuit-completer

board_events.text: Why the cell dies without a salt bridge
As Zn2+ pours in, the anode beaker turns net-positive and repels further oxidation.
As Cu2+ is consumed, the cathode beaker turns net-negative.
Bridge feeds anions to the anode, cations to the cathode: both build-ups neutralised.

board_events.text: It completes the circuit internally, the way the wire completes it externally.
Pull the bridge out and the voltmeter drops to $0$ instantly.

segments.text: The salt bridge does its job quietly but it is indispensable. Let's see exactly what it fixes.
As zinc ions pour into the anode beaker, that solution would turn net-positive, and a positive solution repels any further zinc from oxidising.
Meanwhile the cathode beaker keeps losing copper ions as they plate out, so it would turn net-negative.
The bridge, usually a gel of potassium chloride or potassium nitrate, feeds anions toward the anode and cations toward the cathode, neutralising both build-ups so the reaction keeps running.
Picture it here: anions drift left to cancel the positive anode side, cations drift right to top up the depleted cathode side.
So the bridge completes the circuit on the inside, exactly the way the metal wire completes it on the outside.
<excited>And here is the dramatic proof:</excited> pull the salt bridge out, and the voltmeter drops to zero the instant you do it. Charge piles up, and everyone stops moving.
Salt bridge अपना काम चुपचाप करता है पर यह indispensable है। देखते हैं यह exactly क्या fix करता है।
जैसे-जैसे zinc ions anode beaker में भरते हैं, वह solution net-positive हो जाता है, और positive solution आगे किसी भी zinc को oxidise होने से रोकता है।
उधर cathode beaker से copper ions plate out होकर कम होते जाते हैं, तो वह net-negative हो जाता।
Bridge, आम तौर पर potassium chloride या potassium nitrate का gel, anions को anode की ओर और cations को cathode की ओर भेजता है, दोनों build-ups neutralise करके reaction चलती रखता है।
यहाँ देखो: anions left जाकर positive anode side cancel करते हैं, cations right जाकर घटे हुए cathode side को top up करते हैं।
तो bridge circuit को अंदर से complete करता है, बिल्कुल जैसे metal wire उसे बाहर से complete करता है।
<excited>और यह रहा dramatic proof:</excited> salt bridge बाहर निकालो, और voltmeter उसी पल zero पर गिर जाता है। Charge pile up हो जाता है और सब कुछ रुक जाता है।

segments.text: There is a neat way to rank every species' eagerness to be reduced: the electrochemical series, a table of standard electrode potentials. Read it like a leaderboard.
The species with the most positive potential sits at the top. It grabs electrons hardest, which makes it the strongest oxidising agent.
The species with the most negative potential sits at the bottom. It gives up electrons most readily, which makes it the strongest reducing agent.
Here is the ranking laid out vertically, with potential falling as you go down.
Fluorine sits at the very top, the fiercest electron-grabber. Lithium metal sits at the very bottom, the most generous electron-giver.
<curious>Why memorise this?</curious> Because this single table lets you predict, at a glance, which metal will displace another and which way any cell will run.

As you slide down the table the reduction potential falls: the species on the left become weaker oxidisers, and the metals on the right become stronger reducers. It is a genuine who-outbids-whom for electrons.
हर species की reduce होने की eagerness को rank करने का एक neat तरीका है: electrochemical series, standard electrode potentials की एक table। इसे एक leaderboard की तरह पढ़ो।
सबसे positive potential वाली species top पर होती है। वह electrons सबसे ज़ोर से पकड़ती है, यानी strongest oxidising agent।
सबसे negative potential वाली species bottom पर होती है। वह electrons सबसे आसानी से देती है, यानी strongest reducing agent।
यह रही ranking, vertically, जिसमें नीचे जाते-जाते potential घटता जाता है।
Fluorine बिल्कुल top पर, सबसे तगड़ा electron-grabber। Lithium metal बिल्कुल bottom पर, सबसे उदार electron-giver।
<curious>इसे याद क्यों करें?</curious> क्योंकि यह अकेली table एक नज़र में बता देती है कि कौन सा metal किसे displace करेगा और कोई भी cell किस direction में चलेगी।

Table में नीचे जाते-जाते reduction potential गिरता है: left वाली species कमज़ोर oxidisers बनती हैं और right वाले metals stronger reducers। यह सच में electrons के लिए कौन-किसको-outbid-करता-है वाला मामला है।

sections.title: Why we need a zero: the Standard Hydrogen Electrode

board_events.text: You can never measure a single electrode alone
Only the difference between two electrodes is measurable, like altitude above a chosen sea level.
Chemistry's sea level = Standard Hydrogen Electrode, assigned exactly $0$ V.

segments.text: Now a deep point. We can never measure the potential of a single electrode in isolation. We can only measure the difference between two.
It is exactly like altitude. You cannot state a height in absolute terms; you can only give it relative to a chosen sea level.
Chemistry's sea level is the Standard Hydrogen Electrode, the S H E, which we assign a potential of exactly zero volts by convention.
Here is what it looks like: an inert platinum electrode with hydrogen gas bubbling over it, dipped in an acidic solution.
Run at standard conditions, that means one molar hydrogen ions, hydrogen gas at one bar, and two hundred ninety eight kelvin, this electrode is our universal zero.
To find any unknown standard electrode potential, you couple that electrode to the S H E and read the cell e m f. Because the left electrode is zero, the reading is the unknown's potential directly.

<whisper>One practical secret:</whisper> the S H E is fiddly, needing pure dry hydrogen at exactly one bar, so labs lean on easier secondary references, the calomel electrode and the silver silver-chloride electrode, both pre-calibrated back to this zero.
अब एक deep point। हम किसी single electrode का potential अकेले कभी measure नहीं कर सकते। हम सिर्फ़ दो electrodes का difference measure कर सकते हैं।
यह बिल्कुल altitude जैसा है। आप height को absolute terms में नहीं बता सकते; सिर्फ़ किसी चुने हुए sea level के relative बता सकते हैं।
Chemistry का sea level है Standard Hydrogen Electrode, यानी S H E, जिसे convention से हम exactly zero volts potential देते हैं।
यह ऐसा दिखता है: एक inert platinum electrode जिस पर hydrogen gas bubble कर रही है, एक acidic solution में डूबा हुआ।
Standard conditions पर चलाओ — यानी one molar hydrogen ions, one bar पर hydrogen gas, और two hundred ninety eight kelvin — तो यह electrode हमारा universal zero बन जाता है।
किसी भी unknown standard electrode potential को निकालने के लिए उस electrode को S H E से couple करो और cell e m f पढ़ो। चूँकि left electrode zero है, reading सीधे unknown का potential है।

<whisper>एक practical secret:</whisper> S H E झंझट वाला है, इसे exactly one bar पर pure dry hydrogen चाहिए, तो labs आसान secondary references इस्तेमाल करती हैं — calomel electrode और silver silver-chloride electrode, दोनों इसी zero से pre-calibrated।

board_events.text: Correcting $E^\circ$ for real concentrations
Q encodes how far actual concentrations sit from the standard state.
This bridge converts a thermodynamic statement into an electrical one.

board_events.text: $0.0591$ bakes in $T=298$ K; it is per-electron, so divide by $n$.

segments.text: Standard potentials are quoted for a very specific situation: all ions at one molar, gases at one bar, and two hundred ninety eight kelvin. Real cells rarely sit there, so we need a correction. That correction is the Nernst equation. Let's derive it.
Start from thermodynamics: the Gibbs energy of a reaction equals its standard value plus R T times the natural log of the reaction quotient Q.
Why this step? Because Q encodes how far the actual concentrations sit from the standard state. It is the thermodynamic correction for non-standard conditions.
Now substitute the electrical expressions: the Gibbs energy equals minus n F E, and the standard Gibbs energy equals minus n F E standard.
Why this substitution? This is the bridge that converts a thermodynamic statement into an electrical one, the whole reason a cell can be analysed with Gibbs energy.
Follow the algebra on the board: substitute, then divide through by minus n F, and convert natural log to base-ten log using the factor two point three zero three.

For a metal-ion electrode, the solid metal has activity one and never enters Q, so the electrode potential equals E standard minus zero point zero five nine one over n, times log of one over the metal-ion concentration.

<whisper>Examiners love this:</whisper> the constant zero point zero five nine one already bakes in the temperature of two hundred ninety eight kelvin, and it is per-electron, so you must divide it by n.

Standard potentials एक बहुत specific situation के लिए quote होते हैं: सारे ions one molar, gases one bar, और two hundred ninety eight kelvin। Real cells शायद ही वहाँ बैठती हैं, तो एक correction चाहिए। वही correction है Nernst equation। इसे derive करते हैं।
Thermodynamics से शुरू: किसी reaction की Gibbs energy बराबर होती है उसकी standard value plus R T गुणा reaction quotient Q का natural log।
यह step क्यों? क्योंकि Q बताता है कि actual concentrations standard state से कितनी दूर हैं। यह non-standard conditions का thermodynamic correction है।
अब electrical expressions substitute करो: Gibbs energy बराबर minus n F E, और standard Gibbs energy बराबर minus n F E standard।
यह substitution क्यों? यही वह bridge है जो thermodynamic statement को electrical में बदल देता है — यही पूरी वजह है कि cell को Gibbs energy से analyse किया जा सकता है।
Board पर algebra follow करो: substitute करो, फिर minus n F से divide करो, और natural log को base-ten log में two point three zero three factor से बदलो।

Metal-ion electrode के लिए solid metal की activity one होती है और वह Q में कभी नहीं आता, तो electrode potential बराबर E standard minus zero point zero five nine one over n, गुणा metal-ion concentration के reciprocal का log।
<whisper>Examiners को यह बहुत पसंद है:</whisper> constant zero point zero five nine one में two hundred ninety eight kelvin पहले से बेक्ड है, और यह per-electron है, तो इसे n से divide करना ज़रूरी है।

board_events.text: At equilibrium there is no net driving force: $E_{cell}=0$ and $Q=K_c$.
Equilibrium constants near $K\sim 10^{37}$ drop out of one voltmeter reading.

segments.text: Now scale up from one electrode to a full cell. Write the Nernst equation for the cathode and the anode separately, then subtract, since the cell potential is cathode minus anode.
The two log terms combine into a single Q for the overall reaction, giving the workhorse form: cell potential equals standard cell potential minus zero point zero five nine one over n, times log Q.
As the cell discharges, products accumulate, so Q rises, and the cell potential falls.
The board shows this fall: plot cell potential against log Q and you get a straight line sloping down.
Why must it stop? Eventually the reaction reaches equilibrium: there is no longer any net driving force, so the cell potential is zero and Q equals the equilibrium constant K c.
Set the cell potential to zero, and out drops a beautiful relation: the standard cell potential equals zero point zero five nine one over n, times log of K c.

<excited>This is genuinely powerful.</excited> Equilibrium constants almost impossible to measure directly, think of a K around ten to the thirty-seventh, drop straight out of a single voltmeter reading.
अब एक electrode से पूरी cell तक scale up करो। Cathode और anode के लिए Nernst equation अलग-अलग लिखो, फिर subtract करो, क्योंकि cell potential बराबर cathode minus anode।

दोनों log terms overall reaction के एक single Q में combine हो जाते हैं, जिससे workhorse form मिलती है: cell potential बराबर standard cell potential minus zero point zero five nine one over n, गुणा log Q।
जैसे-जैसे cell discharge होती है, products जमा होते हैं, तो Q बढ़ता है और cell potential गिरता है।
Board यह गिरावट दिखाता है: cell potential को log Q के against plot करो और नीचे की ओर ढलती एक straight line मिलती है।
यह रुकना क्यों ज़रूरी है? आख़िरकार reaction equilibrium पर पहुँचती है: अब कोई net driving force नहीं बचती, तो cell potential zero हो जाता है और Q बराबर equilibrium constant K c।
Cell potential को zero रखो, और एक ख़ूबसूरत relation निकलती है: standard cell potential बराबर zero point zero five nine one over n, गुणा K c का log।
<excited>यह सच में powerful है।</excited> जो equilibrium constants सीधे measure करना लगभग नामुमकिन है — सोचो K करीब ten to the thirty-seventh — वे एक single voltmeter reading से सीधे निकल आते हैं।

segments.text: Exam questions often hand you a cell as a line of symbols. Here is how to read it, using the I U P A C convention.
The anode always goes on the left and the cathode on the right. A single vertical bar marks a phase boundary; a double vertical bar marks the salt bridge.
Look at the annotated notation: nickel and its ion on the left, silver ion and silver on the right, separated by the double-bar salt bridge.
The procedure: write the left electrode as an oxidation and the right as a reduction, then add the half-reactions, balancing the electrons carefully.
Then compute the standard cell potential as E standard of the right electrode minus E standard of the left.
If that value comes out positive, the reaction as written is spontaneous and the notation is a correct galvanic cell.

One more piece: not every half-cell has a reactive metal. For couples that live entirely in solution or involve a gas, such as iron-three iron-two, or the hydrogen couple, an inert electrode like platinum or gold just ferries electrons in and out without joining the chemistry.
Exam questions अक्सर cell को symbols की एक line के रूप में देते हैं। इसे पढ़ने का तरीका यह है, I U P A C convention से।
Anode हमेशा left पर और cathode right पर। एक single vertical bar phase boundary दिखाती है; एक double vertical bar salt bridge।
Annotated notation देखो: left पर nickel और उसका ion, right पर silver ion और silver, बीच में double-bar salt bridge।
Procedure: left electrode को oxidation लिखो और right को reduction, फिर half-reactions को electrons balance करते हुए add करो।
फिर standard cell potential निकालो — right electrode के E standard minus left के E standard।
अगर वह value positive आती है, तो जैसा लिखा है reaction spontaneous है और notation एक correct galvanic cell है।

एक और बात: हर half-cell में reactive metal नहीं होता। जो couples पूरी तरह solution में हैं या gas वाले हैं — जैसे iron-three iron-two, या hydrogen couple — वहाँ platinum या gold जैसा inert electrode बस electrons अंदर-बाहर ले जाता है, chemistry में शामिल हुए बिना।

sections.title: The complete toolkit: potentials, Nernst, Gibbs, Kc

board_events.text: Every formula this subtopic rests on
Outside 298 K, revert to the full $\frac{2.303RT}{nF}$ form.

segments.text: Let's consolidate the whole toolkit onto one board, so every numerical has its formula in one place.
First, the standard cell potential: it is the cathode's standard potential minus the anode's, which is the same as right minus left, both taken as reduction potentials.
Second, the general Nernst equation: cell potential equals standard cell potential minus two point three zero three R T over n F, times log Q.
Third, at two hundred ninety eight kelvin this collapses to the workhorse form, with the constant zero point zero five nine one over n in front of log Q.
Fourth, the Gibbs links: the reaction Gibbs energy is minus n F times the cell potential, and the standard version is minus n F times the standard cell potential.
Fifth, the equilibrium bridge: log of K c equals n times the standard cell potential, divided by zero point zero five nine one.

Memorise this: zero point zero five nine one is two point three zero three times eight point three one four times two hundred ninety eight, all over ninety six thousand four hundred eighty five, the Faraday constant.
And a caution: the clean constant only holds at two hundred ninety eight kelvin. Outside that temperature, you must revert to the full two point three zero three R T over n F form.
पूरी toolkit एक board पर consolidate कर लेते हैं, ताकि हर numerical का formula एक ही जगह मिले।
पहला, standard cell potential: यह cathode के standard potential minus anode का है, जो right minus left के बराबर है, दोनों reduction potentials के रूप में।
दूसरा, general Nernst equation: cell potential बराबर standard cell potential minus two point three zero three R T over n F, गुणा log Q।
तीसरा, two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर यह workhorse form में सिमट जाता है, जिसमें log Q के आगे constant zero point zero five nine one over n होता है।
चौथा, Gibbs links: reaction Gibbs energy बराबर minus n F गुणा cell potential, और standard version बराबर minus n F गुणा standard cell potential।
पाँचवाँ, equilibrium bridge: K c का log बराबर n गुणा standard cell potential, zero point zero five nine one से divided।

यह याद रखो: zero point zero five nine one बराबर है two point three zero three गुणा eight point three one four गुणा two hundred ninety eight, पूरे का ninety six thousand four hundred eighty five से — यानी Faraday constant से — भाग।
और एक caution: यह clean constant सिर्फ़ two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर लागू है। उस temperature के बाहर, full two point three zero three R T over n F form पर लौटना पड़ता है।

board_events.text: More negative potential oxidises: nickel is the anode, silver the cathode.

segments.text: Let's put the theory to work. We are given the silver couple at plus zero point eight zero volts and the nickel couple at minus zero point two five volts. Set up the galvanic cell, write its reaction, and find the standard cell potential.
Write down what we have: silver's standard reduction potential is plus zero point eight zero volts, and nickel's is minus zero point two five volts.
Here is the cell we are about to justify: nickel on the left, silver on the right.
The rule is that the more negative reduction potential is the one that oxidises. Nickel's minus zero point two five is more negative, so nickel is the anode and silver is the cathode.
Write the anode as an oxidation: solid nickel gives a nickel two-plus ion and two electrons.
Write the cathode as a reduction: a silver ion plus one electron gives solid silver. To balance electrons we multiply this by two.
Add them for the overall reaction: solid nickel plus two silver ions give a nickel ion plus two solid silvers.

Finally the standard cell potential is cathode minus anode: zero point eight zero minus minus zero point two five, which is one point zero five volts. The positive value confirms the reaction is spontaneous.

अब theory को काम पर लगाते हैं। हमें silver couple plus zero point eight zero volts और nickel couple minus zero point two five volts दिए हैं। Galvanic cell set up करो, reaction लिखो, और standard cell potential निकालो।
जो दिया है वह लिखो: silver का standard reduction potential plus zero point eight zero volts, और nickel का minus zero point two five volts।
यह रही वह cell जिसे हम justify करने वाले हैं: left पर nickel, right पर silver।
Rule यह है कि ज़्यादा negative reduction potential वाला oxidise होता है। Nickel का minus zero point two five ज़्यादा negative है, तो nickel anode है और silver cathode।
Anode को oxidation लिखो: solid nickel देता है एक nickel two-plus ion और दो electrons।
Cathode को reduction लिखो: एक silver ion plus one electron देता है solid silver। Electrons balance करने के लिए इसे दो से multiply करो।
इन्हें add करके overall reaction: solid nickel plus दो silver ions देते हैं एक nickel ion और दो solid silvers।

आख़िर में standard cell potential बराबर cathode minus anode: zero point eight zero minus minus zero point two five, यानी one point zero five volts। Positive value confirm करती है कि reaction spontaneous है।

segments.text: Two quick examples that reward thinking over grinding. First, the NEET speed trap.
For a zinc-copper cell, both the zinc-ion and copper-ion concentrations are simultaneously doubled. How does the cell potential change?
The trap is that students reflexively reach for the Nernst equation and start computing two log terms. Instead, look at Q. It is the ratio of zinc-ion to copper-ion concentration.

<chuckle>Doubling both leaves the ratio untouched.</chuckle> Two over two cancels, so Q is unchanged, and therefore the cell potential is unchanged. No calculation needed, just recognise Q is a ratio.

Now a JEE Main example on the Gibbs and equilibrium links. A cell is built from iron at minus zero point four four volts and copper at plus zero point three four volts. Find the standard cell potential, the standard Gibbs energy, and the equilibrium constant.
Iron is more negative so it oxidises; n is two. The standard cell potential is zero point three four minus minus zero point four four, which is zero point seven eight volts.

The standard Gibbs energy is minus n F times the cell potential: minus two times ninety six thousand four hundred eighty five times zero point seven eight, about minus one hundred fifty point five kilojoules per mole.

And log of K c is n times the cell potential over zero point zero five nine one, which is two times zero point seven eight over zero point zero five nine one, giving twenty six point four. So K c is about two point five times ten to the twenty-sixth, a huge number telling us the reaction runs essentially to completion.
दो quick examples जो grinding से ज़्यादा thinking को reward करते हैं। पहला, NEET speed trap।
एक zinc-copper cell में zinc-ion और copper-ion दोनों की concentrations एक साथ double कर दी जाती हैं। Cell potential कैसे बदलेगा?
Trap यह है कि students reflexively Nernst equation उठा लेते हैं और दो log terms compute करने लगते हैं। इसके बजाय Q देखो। यह zinc-ion और copper-ion concentration का ratio है।
<chuckle>दोनों को double करने से ratio अछूता रहता है।</chuckle> दो बटा दो cancel हो जाता है, तो Q unchanged है, और इसलिए cell potential unchanged। कोई calculation नहीं, बस पहचानो कि Q एक ratio है।

अब Gibbs और equilibrium links पर एक JEE Main example। एक cell बनती है iron minus zero point four four volts और copper plus zero point three four volts से। Standard cell potential, standard Gibbs energy, और equilibrium constant निकालो।
Iron ज़्यादा negative है तो वह oxidise होता है; n है two। Standard cell potential बराबर zero point three four minus minus zero point four four, यानी zero point seven eight volts।

Standard Gibbs energy बराबर minus n F गुणा cell potential: minus two गुणा ninety six thousand four hundred eighty five गुणा zero point seven eight, करीब minus one hundred fifty point five kilojoules per mole।

और K c का log बराबर n गुणा cell potential बटा zero point zero five nine one, यानी two गुणा zero point seven eight बटा zero point zero five nine one, जो देता है twenty six point four। तो K c करीब two point five गुणा ten to the twenty-sixth — एक huge number जो बताता है reaction essentially completion तक चलती है।

board_events.text: Dead means $E_{cell}=0$, i.e. $Q=K_c$.

segments.text: Now a full JEE Advanced Nernst calculation with real concentrations. Take a zinc-silver cell with zinc-ion at zero point one zero molar and silver-ion at zero point zero one zero molar.
We are given zinc at minus zero point seven six volts, silver at plus zero point eight zero volts, and n equal to two.
The board lays out all three steps: the standard potential, the reaction quotient, and the Nernst-corrected potential.
First the standard cell potential: zero point eight zero minus minus zero point seven six, which is one point five six volts.

Next the reaction quotient. The reaction is zinc plus two silver ions, so Q is the zinc-ion concentration over the silver-ion concentration squared. That is zero point one zero over zero point zero one zero squared, which equals one point zero times ten cubed.

Now apply Nernst: one point five six minus zero point zero five nine one over two times log of ten cubed. The log is three, so we subtract zero point zero eight eight seven, giving a cell potential of one point four seven volts.
For part b, dead means the cell potential is zero, which happens when Q equals the equilibrium constant K c.

<whisper>Here is the striking finish:</whisper> log of K c is two times one point five six over zero point zero five nine one, which is fifty two point eight, so the ratio must climb to about six times ten to the fifty-second before the cell stops. Practically, the silver ions are consumed almost entirely first. That is the rigorous meaning of discharging until equilibrium.
अब real concentrations के साथ एक full JEE Advanced Nernst calculation। एक zinc-silver cell लो जिसमें zinc-ion zero point one zero molar और silver-ion zero point zero one zero molar है।
हमें दिया है zinc minus zero point seven six volts, silver plus zero point eight zero volts, और n बराबर two।
Board तीनों steps रखता है: standard potential, reaction quotient, और Nernst-corrected potential।
पहले standard cell potential: zero point eight zero minus minus zero point seven six, यानी one point five six volts।

फिर reaction quotient। Reaction है zinc plus दो silver ions, तो Q बराबर zinc-ion concentration बटा silver-ion concentration का square। यानी zero point one zero बटा zero point zero one zero का square, जो बराबर one point zero गुणा ten cubed।

अब Nernst लगाओ: one point five six minus zero point zero five nine one over two गुणा ten cubed का log। Log है three, तो हम zero point zero eight eight seven घटाते हैं, जिससे cell potential one point four seven volts।
Part b के लिए, dead का मतलब cell potential zero, जो तब होता है जब Q बराबर equilibrium constant K c।

<whisper>यह रहा striking finish:</whisper> K c का log बराबर two गुणा one point five six बटा zero point zero five nine one, यानी fifty two point eight, तो cell रुकने से पहले ratio को करीब six गुणा ten to the fifty-second तक चढ़ना पड़ता है। Practically, silver ions पहले लगभग पूरे consume हो जाते हैं। यही है equilibrium तक discharge होने का rigorous मतलब।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for cells and Nernst

board_events.text: Where marks are quietly lost
Galvanic: anode $-$, cathode $+$. Electrolytic flips the signs.
Forgetting $n$ in the log term: the constant is $\frac{0.0591}{n}$, not $0.0591$.
For $n=2$ it is $0.02955$. Always read $n$ from the balanced electron count first.
Pure solids and liquids have activity 1: never put them into $Q$.
Do not confuse $E_{cell}=0$ (equilibrium) with $E^\circ_{cell}=0$.
Pro-tip: for "does the value change?", inspect $Q$; don't compute.
A positive $E^\circ_{cell}$ and a negative $\Delta_r G^\circ$ always travel together.

segments.text: Let's close this subtopic with the traps that quietly cost easy marks.
First, sign confusion. In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and the cathode is positive. In an electrolytic cell the signs flip. Mixing the two conventions is a guaranteed mark-loss.
Second, forgetting n in the log term. The Nernst constant is zero point zero five nine one over n, not just zero point zero five nine one.
For n equal to two, that constant is zero point zero two nine five five. Always identify n from the balanced electron count before you plug anything in.
Third, putting solids or liquids into Q. Pure metals, pure solids, and pure liquids all have activity one and never appear in the reaction quotient. Only dissolved ions and gas pressures do.
Fourth, and this is the deep one: never confuse the actual cell potential being zero at equilibrium with the standard cell potential being zero. The standard value is a fixed nonzero constant.

<whisper>Here is the pro-tip that saves time:</whisper> for any "does the value change?" question, do not compute. Inspect Q. If a concentration change leaves the ratio in Q untouched, the potential is unchanged.
And for spontaneity questions, remember that a positive standard cell potential and a negative standard Gibbs energy always travel together. Check one, and you instantly know the other.
इस subtopic को उन traps के साथ close करते हैं जो चुपचाप easy marks ले जाते हैं।
पहला, sign confusion। Galvanic cell में anode negative और cathode positive। Electrolytic cell में signs flip हो जाते हैं। दोनों conventions mix करना guaranteed mark-loss है।
दूसरा, log term में n भूल जाना। Nernst constant है zero point zero five nine one over n, सिर्फ़ zero point zero five nine one नहीं।
n बराबर two के लिए वह constant है zero point zero two nine five five। कुछ भी plug करने से पहले हमेशा balanced electron count से n पहचानो।
तीसरा, solids या liquids को Q में डालना। Pure metals, pure solids, और pure liquids सबकी activity one होती है और वे reaction quotient में कभी नहीं आते। सिर्फ़ dissolved ions और gas pressures आते हैं।
चौथा, और यह deep वाला है: equilibrium पर actual cell potential zero होने को standard cell potential zero होने से कभी मत confuse करो। Standard value एक fixed nonzero constant है।

<whisper>यह रहा वह pro-tip जो time बचाता है:</whisper> किसी भी "does the value change?" question के लिए compute मत करो। Q देखो। अगर concentration change से Q का ratio अछूता रहता है, तो potential unchanged है।
और spontaneity questions के लिए याद रखो कि positive standard cell potential और negative standard Gibbs energy हमेशा साथ चलते हैं। एक check करो, दूसरा तुरंत पता चल जाता है।

board_events.text: Cations crawl to the cathode, anions to the anode, physically ferrying charge.
Warming a metal lowers conductance; warming a solution raises it.
Conduction here is inseparable from chemistry: ions are consumed and released at electrodes.

segments.text: You already know metals conduct, but look closely at how. In a metal the copper atoms stay put while a sea of free electrons drifts through them. Nothing material travels from one end of the wire to the other, only the electrons shuffle. That is metallic conduction.
Hold that picture: the lattice is fixed, and only a thin stream of electrons moves.
Now dissolve common salt in water and dip in two electrodes. Current flows again, but the mechanism is completely different. There are no free electrons here at all.
Instead the dissolved sodium and chloride ions themselves migrate, as the panels show: cations crawl toward the cathode, anions toward the anode.
The ions physically ferry charge across the solution. This is electrolytic, or ionic, conduction, and it is what this whole subtopic is about.

<curious>Here is a reversal worth noticing.</curious> Warming a metal makes its lattice vibrate and obstruct electrons, so conductance falls. Warming a solution loosens the crowd of ions, so conductance rises.
And a second consequence: conduction here is inseparable from chemistry. Ions are actually consumed and released at the electrodes, which never happens in a plain metal wire.

आप जानते हैं कि metals conduct करते हैं, पर ध्यान से देखो कैसे। Metal में copper atoms अपनी जगह टिके रहते हैं जबकि free electrons का एक sea उनके बीच से बहता है। Wire के एक सिरे से दूसरे तक कोई material नहीं जाता, सिर्फ़ electrons shuffle करते हैं। यह metallic conduction है।
यह picture पकड़ो: lattice fixed है, और सिर्फ़ electrons की एक पतली धारा move करती है।
अब पानी में common salt घोलो और दो electrodes डालो। Current फिर बहती है, पर mechanism बिल्कुल अलग है। यहाँ free electrons हैं ही नहीं।
इसके बजाय घुले हुए sodium और chloride ions ख़ुद migrate करते हैं, जैसा panels दिखाते हैं: cations cathode की ओर, anions anode की ओर।
Ions physically charge को solution के पार ले जाते हैं। यह electrolytic, यानी ionic, conduction है, और यही पूरा subtopic इसी के बारे में है।

<curious>यहाँ एक reversal ध्यान देने लायक है।</curious> Metal को गरम करो तो lattice vibrate करके electrons को रोकती है, conductance गिरता है। Solution को गरम करो तो ions की भीड़ ढीली होती है, conductance बढ़ता है।
और एक दूसरा consequence: यहाँ conduction chemistry से अलग नहीं है। Electrodes पर ions सच में consume और release होते हैं, जो plain metal wire में कभी नहीं होता।

sections.title: From resistance to conductivity and the cell constant

board_events.text: Factor geometry out of resistance
A column of solution has resistance $R$; its reciprocal is conductance $G$.
But $R$ depends on shape: fat and short conducts better than thin and long.

board_events.caption: Geometry of the solution column

board_events.text: Cell constant $G^{*}=l/A$ is found by calibrating with standard KCl.
$\kappa$ is conductivity, unit S cm$^{-1}$: think "conductance per unit cube."

segments.text: To measure how well a solution conducts, we borrow the language of resistors. A column of solution has a resistance R, and its reciprocal is the conductance G.
So conductance is simply one over resistance, measured in siemens, the old name for which was the mho.
Here is the resistance law: R equals resistivity rho times length over area. Taking the reciprocal gives conductance.
But R depends on the shape of the column. A fat, short column conducts far better than a thin, long one, so raw resistance is not an intrinsic property of the liquid.
The diagram shows the two geometric factors: the length between electrodes, and the cross-sectional area.
So we factor the geometry out. Conductivity kappa equals one over resistivity, which equals conductance times length over area, that is conductance times the cell constant.

<whisper>A practical secret:</whisper> we never measure length and area directly, because a real cell has messy fringing fields. Instead we calibrate the cell with a standard potassium chloride solution of known conductivity and back out the cell constant.
Kappa is the conductivity, or specific conductance, with the practical unit siemens per centimetre. Think of it as conductance per unit cube of solution, an intrinsic material property.
यह measure करने के लिए कि solution कितना अच्छा conduct करता है, हम resistors की भाषा उधार लेते हैं। Solution के एक column की resistance R होती है, और उसका reciprocal conductance G।
तो conductance बस one over resistance है, siemens में मापा जाता है, जिसका पुराना नाम mho था।
यह रहा resistance law: R बराबर resistivity rho गुणा length बटा area। Reciprocal लेने पर conductance मिलता है।
पर R column के shape पर depend करता है। एक मोटा, छोटा column पतले, लंबे से कहीं बेहतर conduct करता है, तो raw resistance liquid की intrinsic property नहीं है।
Diagram दो geometric factors दिखाता है: electrodes के बीच की length, और cross-sectional area।
तो हम geometry को factor out करते हैं। Conductivity kappa बराबर one over resistivity, जो बराबर conductance गुणा length बटा area, यानी conductance गुणा cell constant।

<whisper>एक practical secret:</whisper> हम length और area कभी सीधे measure नहीं करते, क्योंकि असली cell में fringing fields गड़बड़ होते हैं। इसके बजाय हम cell को known conductivity वाले standard potassium chloride solution से calibrate करके cell constant निकालते हैं।
Kappa है conductivity, या specific conductance, जिसका practical unit siemens per centimetre है। इसे solution के per unit cube की conductance समझो, एक intrinsic material property।

board_events.text: Yet the molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ rises. Why the opposite direction?
$\Lambda_m$ asks a fairer question: fix one mole, however much water it needs.
On dilution that mole's ions spread out, interact less, and each moves more freely.
Holding the AMOUNT fixed instead of the VOLUME is the entire trick.

segments.text: Now meet the subtlety that trips up almost everyone. Take a strong-salt solution and keep diluting it.
The conductivity kappa falls, and that is obvious: you are thinning out the ion crowd, so there are fewer charge-carriers per cubic centimetre.
The diagram makes it concrete: the same ions, now spread through much more water.
Yet the molar conductivity, capital lambda m, rises on dilution. Why the opposite direction? This is the classic exam trap.
Because molar conductivity deliberately asks a fairer question. It says: if I take exactly one mole of the electrolyte, however much water that needs, how well does that fixed amount conduct?
On dilution, that one mole's ions spread into a larger volume and interact with each other less, so each ion moves more freely. Molar conductivity therefore climbs.
<excited>Here is the one line to burn in:</excited> holding the amount fixed instead of the volume fixed is the entire trick. Kappa down, molar conductivity up.
अब वह subtlety मिलो जो लगभग सबको फँसाती है। एक strong-salt solution लो और उसे लगातार dilute करते जाओ।
Conductivity kappa गिरता है, और यह obvious है: आप ion की भीड़ पतली कर रहे हो, तो per cubic centimetre charge-carriers कम हो जाते हैं।
Diagram इसे concrete बना देता है: वही ions, अब कहीं ज़्यादा पानी में फैले हुए।
फिर भी molar conductivity, capital lambda m, dilution पर बढ़ती है। उल्टी direction क्यों? यही classic exam trap है।
क्योंकि molar conductivity जानबूझकर एक fairer सवाल पूछती है। वह कहती है: अगर मैं electrolyte का exactly one mole लूँ, चाहे उसे जितना पानी चाहिए, वह fixed amount कितना अच्छा conduct करता है?
Dilution पर उस one mole के ions बड़े volume में फैल जाते हैं और आपस में कम interact करते हैं, तो हर ion ज़्यादा आज़ादी से move करता है। इसलिए molar conductivity चढ़ती है।
<excited>यह रही burn-in करने वाली एक line:</excited> volume fixed रखने के बजाय amount fixed रखना ही पूरा trick है। Kappa down, molar conductivity up।

board_events.text: The proton relays down a chain of hydrogen-bonded water, like a whisper passed along.
Ordinary ions must shoulder through water, dragging a shell of stuck-on molecules.
Smaller-looking ions can be slower: they hold a bigger hydration shell.
So HCl out-conducts KCl, which out-conducts CH3COONa, at the same concentration.

segments.text: One last piece of intuition explains a lot of exam questions: not all ions move at the same speed.
A bare proton, the hydrogen ion, and a hydroxide ion conduct far better than their tiny size would suggest, because they barely move bodily at all.
The diagram shows why. Instead of travelling, the proton relays down a chain of hydrogen-bonded water molecules.
It is like a message whispered along a row of people without anyone actually changing seats. This relay is enormously faster than pushing a whole ion through the liquid.
Ordinary ions such as sodium or chloride get no such shortcut. They must shoulder their way through the water, dragging a shell of stuck-on water molecules with them.
<curious>Here is a counterintuitive twist:</curious> a smaller-looking ion is sometimes slower, because it holds a bigger hydration shell and so drags more water.

That is why hydrochloric acid out-conducts potassium chloride, which out-conducts sodium acetate, all at the same concentration. The cation and anion identities, not just their count, set the molar conductivity.
एक आख़िरी intuition बहुत सारे exam questions समझा देती है: सारे ions एक ही speed से move नहीं करते।
एक bare proton, यानी hydrogen ion, और एक hydroxide ion अपने छोटे size से कहीं बेहतर conduct करते हैं, क्योंकि वे bodily लगभग move करते ही नहीं।
Diagram बताता है क्यों। Travel करने के बजाय proton hydrogen-bonded water molecules की एक chain के साथ relay करता है।
यह ऐसा है जैसे लोगों की कतार में एक message फुसफुसाते हुए आगे बढ़े, बिना किसी के seat बदले। यह relay पूरे ion को liquid में धकेलने से कहीं तेज़ है।
Sodium या chloride जैसे ordinary ions को ऐसा कोई shortcut नहीं मिलता। उन्हें पानी में धक्का देकर आगे बढ़ना पड़ता है, अपने साथ चिपके water molecules का shell घसीटते हुए।
<curious>यहाँ एक counterintuitive मोड़ है:</curious> छोटा दिखने वाला ion कभी-कभी slower होता है, क्योंकि वह बड़ा hydration shell पकड़े रहता है और ज़्यादा पानी घसीटता है।

इसीलिए hydrochloric acid, potassium chloride से ज़्यादा conduct करता है, जो sodium acetate से ज़्यादा, सब एक ही concentration पर। Cation और anion की पहचान, सिर्फ़ उनकी गिनती नहीं, molar conductivity तय करती है।

sections.title: Strong versus weak electrolytes: the square-root law

board_events.text: Reading $\Lambda^{\circ}_m$ off a graph
For a strong electrolyte this is a nearly straight line, extrapolated to $c\to 0$.

board_events.text: A weak electrolyte curves sharply upward near $c=0$ and cannot be extrapolated.
The square-root law holds only for strong electrolytes at low concentration.
$\Lambda^{\circ}_m$ is the limiting molar conductivity: the value as $c\to 0$.

segments.text: How do we get the limiting molar conductivity, the value at infinite dilution? For a strong electrolyte, a simple law does the job.
The Debye-Huckel-Onsager form says the molar conductivity equals the limiting molar conductivity minus a constant A times the square root of concentration.
For a strong electrolyte this is a nearly straight line with a gentle negative slope, so you simply extrapolate it back to zero concentration to read off the limiting value.
Look at the graph: the strong electrolyte, potassium chloride, is the gentle line meeting the axis cleanly at the limiting molar conductivity.

But the weak electrolyte, acetic acid, is very low and almost flat across most of the range, then sweeps steeply upward as concentration approaches zero, never reaching the axis cleanly. You cannot extrapolate it.
So remember the condition: the clean square-root law holds only for strong electrolytes at low concentration. Weak electrolytes curve sharply and break it.
The limiting molar conductivity, written lambda-m-nought, is just the value the molar conductivity approaches as concentration goes to zero, where ions are so far apart they ignore each other.
Limiting molar conductivity, यानी infinite dilution पर value, कैसे निकालें? Strong electrolyte के लिए एक simple law काम कर देता है।
Debye-Huckel-Onsager form कहती है कि molar conductivity बराबर limiting molar conductivity minus एक constant A गुणा concentration का square root।
Strong electrolyte के लिए यह एक हल्की negative slope वाली लगभग straight line है, तो आप उसे बस zero concentration तक extrapolate करके limiting value पढ़ लेते हो।
Graph देखो: strong electrolyte, potassium chloride, वह gentle line है जो axis को साफ़-साफ़ limiting molar conductivity पर मिलती है।

पर weak electrolyte, acetic acid, ज़्यादातर range में बहुत नीचे और लगभग flat रहता है, फिर concentration zero की ओर जाते ही तेज़ी से ऊपर उठ जाता है, axis को साफ़ नहीं छूता। इसे extrapolate नहीं कर सकते।
तो condition याद रखो: clean square-root law सिर्फ़ strong electrolytes के लिए low concentration पर लागू है। Weak electrolytes तेज़ी से curve होकर इसे तोड़ देते हैं।
Limiting molar conductivity, lambda-m-nought, बस वह value है जिसकी ओर molar conductivity तब बढ़ती है जब concentration zero जाता है, जहाँ ions इतने दूर होते हैं कि एक-दूसरे को ignore कर देते हैं।

sections.title: Deriving molar conductivity and the factor of 1000

board_events.text: Why $\Lambda_m = \kappa/c$, and the unit care
$\kappa$ is conductance per unit volume, but solutions pack different amounts in.

board_events.caption: Normalise to one mole

board_events.text: Molarity is mol per 1000 cm$^3$, so $c$ (mol cm$^{-3}$) = molarity/1000.

segments.text: Now let's derive molar conductivity and, more importantly, understand the factor of one thousand that costs students marks.
Kappa is conductance per unit volume. But different solutions pack different amounts of electrolyte into that volume, so kappa alone is an unfair comparison between electrolytes.
So we normalise to one mole. Imagine a slab of solution holding exactly one mole of electrolyte between two large plates, as the diagram shows.

The volume holding one mole is one over the concentration. Since the conductance scales with that volume while kappa is the per-unit-volume conductance, the molar conductivity equals kappa times the volume, which is kappa over c.

Now the unit care. Concentration is almost always quoted as molarity, which is moles per litre, and a litre is one thousand cubic centimetres. So the concentration in moles per cubic centimetre is the molarity divided by one thousand.
Substituting gives the working formula you actually use: molar conductivity equals kappa times one thousand, divided by the molarity.
<whisper>And a conversion to keep handy:</whisper> one siemens centimetre-squared per mole equals ten to the minus four siemens metre-squared per mole, which is how you switch to S I units.
अब molar conductivity derive करते हैं और, उससे भी ज़रूरी, वह one thousand का factor समझते हैं जो students के marks ले जाता है।
Kappa है conductance per unit volume। पर अलग-अलग solutions उस volume में अलग amount electrolyte भरते हैं, तो अकेला kappa electrolytes के बीच unfair comparison है।
तो हम one mole पर normalise करते हैं। एक slab की कल्पना करो जिसमें दो बड़ी plates के बीच exactly one mole electrolyte है, जैसा diagram दिखाता है।

One mole रखने वाला volume है one over concentration। चूँकि conductance उस volume के साथ scale करता है जबकि kappa per-unit-volume conductance है, molar conductivity बराबर kappa गुणा volume, यानी kappa over c।

अब unit care। Concentration लगभग हमेशा molarity में दी जाती है, यानी moles per litre, और एक litre है one thousand cubic centimetres। तो moles per cubic centimetre में concentration बराबर molarity भाग one thousand।
Substitute करने पर वह working formula मिलती है जो आप सच में इस्तेमाल करते हो: molar conductivity बराबर kappa गुणा one thousand, molarity से भाग।
<whisper>और एक conversion हाथ में रखो:</whisper> one siemens centimetre-squared per mole बराबर ten to the minus four siemens metre-squared per mole, इसी से आप S I units में switch करते हो।

sections.title: Kohlrausch's law: weak acids, dissociation and solubility

board_events.text: Independent migration of ions at infinite dilution
A weak acid's curve can't be extrapolated, so build it from strong electrolytes.

board_events.caption: Spectator ions cancel

board_events.text: Same idea gives salt solubility: $S = \kappa_{salt}\times 1000 / \Lambda^{\circ}_m$.

segments.text: Kohlrausch's law is the key that unlocks weak electrolytes. It states that at infinite dilution, each ion contributes to the conductivity independently.
So the limiting molar conductivity is the sum of the ionic conductivities of the cations and anions, each weighted by how many of that ion appear per formula unit.
Since a weak acid's curve shoots up steeply near zero and cannot be extrapolated, we build its limiting value from strong electrolytes we can measure.
The diagram shows the trick, like a thermochemical cycle: take hydrochloric acid plus the sodium salt of the acid, minus sodium chloride.
On the right, the sodium and the chloride contributions cancel exactly, leaving just the hydrogen ion and the acid's anion, which are precisely the ions of the weak acid.

Once you have the limiting value, you get more: the degree of dissociation alpha is the measured molar conductivity over the limiting one, and the dissociation constant follows from Ostwald's law, c alpha squared over one minus alpha.

<excited>And the same idea has a bonus use:</excited> for a sparingly soluble salt, the saturated solution is so dilute it sits at infinite dilution, so its solubility is kappa of the salt times one thousand over the limiting molar conductivity.
Kohlrausch's law वह चाबी है जो weak electrolytes खोल देती है। यह कहती है कि infinite dilution पर हर ion conductivity में independently contribute करता है।
तो limiting molar conductivity, cations और anions की ionic conductivities का योग है, हर एक को इस बात से weight करके कि वह ion per formula unit कितनी बार आता है।
चूँकि weak acid की curve zero के पास तेज़ी से ऊपर जाती है और extrapolate नहीं हो सकती, हम उसकी limiting value measurable strong electrolytes से बनाते हैं।
Diagram trick दिखाता है, एक thermochemical cycle की तरह: hydrochloric acid plus acid का sodium salt, minus sodium chloride।
Right पर, sodium और chloride के contributions exactly cancel हो जाते हैं, बच जाते हैं सिर्फ़ hydrogen ion और acid का anion, जो ठीक weak acid के ions हैं।
Limiting value मिलते ही और मिलता है: degree of dissociation alpha बराबर measured molar conductivity बटा limiting, और dissociation constant Ostwald's law से, c alpha squared बटा one minus alpha।

<excited>और उसी idea का एक bonus use है:</excited> sparingly soluble salt के लिए saturated solution इतना dilute होता है कि वह infinite dilution पर बैठता है, तो उसकी solubility बराबर salt का kappa गुणा one thousand बटा limiting molar conductivity।

sections.title: The conductance toolkit

board_events.text: Every relation this subtopic uses
Units: G in S; $\kappa$ in S cm$^{-1}$; $\Lambda_m$ in S cm$^{2}$ mol$^{-1}$; $G^{*}$ in cm$^{-1}$.
Sparingly soluble salt: $S = \kappa_{salt}\times 1000/\Lambda^{\circ}_m$, then $K_{sp}=S^{2}$ for a 1:1 salt.

segments.text: Let's gather the whole conductance toolkit onto one board.
First the core chain: conductance is one over resistance; and conductivity kappa is conductance times the cell constant, which is length over area.
Second, molar conductivity is kappa times one thousand, divided by the molarity, whenever kappa is in siemens per centimetre and concentration in moles per litre.
Third, for a strong electrolyte, molar conductivity equals the limiting value minus a constant times the square root of concentration, which you extrapolate to get the limiting value.
Fourth, for a weak acid, use Kohlrausch: the limiting value of the acid equals that of hydrochloric acid plus the sodium salt minus sodium chloride.
Fifth, the weak-electrolyte pair: the degree of dissociation is molar conductivity over the limiting value, and the dissociation constant is c alpha squared over one minus alpha.
Keep the units straight: conductance in siemens, kappa in siemens per centimetre, molar conductivity in siemens centimetre-squared per mole, and the cell constant in per centimetre.

And for a sparingly soluble salt, the solubility is kappa of the salt times one thousand over the limiting molar conductivity, and for a one-to-one salt the solubility product is just the solubility squared.
पूरी conductance toolkit एक board पर इकट्ठा कर लेते हैं।
पहले core chain: conductance बराबर one over resistance; और conductivity kappa बराबर conductance गुणा cell constant, जो length over area है।
दूसरा, molar conductivity बराबर kappa गुणा one thousand, molarity से भाग, जब भी kappa siemens per centimetre में हो और concentration moles per litre में।
तीसरा, strong electrolyte के लिए molar conductivity बराबर limiting value minus एक constant गुणा concentration का square root, जिसे extrapolate करके limiting value निकालते हो।
चौथा, weak acid के लिए Kohlrausch इस्तेमाल करो: acid की limiting value बराबर hydrochloric acid plus sodium salt minus sodium chloride।
पाँचवाँ, weak-electrolyte जोड़ी: degree of dissociation बराबर molar conductivity बटा limiting value, और dissociation constant बराबर c alpha squared बटा one minus alpha।
Units सही रखो: conductance siemens में, kappa siemens per centimetre में, molar conductivity siemens centimetre-squared per mole में, और cell constant per centimetre में।
और sparingly soluble salt के लिए solubility बराबर salt का kappa गुणा one thousand बटा limiting molar conductivity, और one-to-one salt के लिए solubility product बस solubility का square।

sections.title: Worked example: kappa and molar conductivity from resistance

board_events.text: CBSE level
0.050 M solution: resistance $220\,\Omega$, cell constant $1.15$ cm$^{-1}$.

board_events.text: Mind the $\times 1000$: forgetting it is the classic slip.

segments.text: Here is a standard C B S E numerical. A conductivity cell filled with a zero point zero five zero molar solution has a resistance of two hundred twenty ohms, and the cell constant is one point one five per centimetre. Find the conductivity and the molar conductivity.
So we are given the concentration, the resistance, and the cell constant. Let's work through it.
The board lays out all three steps in order.
First, conductance is one over resistance: one over two hundred twenty, which is four point five four five times ten to the minus three siemens.

Next, conductivity is conductance times the cell constant: four point five four five times ten to the minus three, times one point one five, giving five point two three times ten to the minus three siemens per centimetre.

Finally, molar conductivity is kappa times one thousand over the molarity: five point two three times ten to the minus three, times one thousand, over zero point zero five zero, which comes to one hundred four point five siemens centimetre-squared per mole.
<whisper>Watch the thousand.</whisper> Forgetting to multiply by one thousand is the single most common slip on this kind of question.

यह रहा एक standard C B S E numerical। एक conductivity cell जिसमें zero point zero five zero molar solution है, उसकी resistance two hundred twenty ohms है, और cell constant one point one five per centimetre। Conductivity और molar conductivity निकालो।
तो हमें concentration, resistance, और cell constant दिए हैं। इसे step by step करते हैं।
Board तीनों steps क्रम से रखता है।
पहले, conductance बराबर one over resistance: one over two hundred twenty, यानी four point five four five times ten to the minus three siemens।

फिर, conductivity बराबर conductance गुणा cell constant: four point five four five times ten to the minus three, गुणा one point one five, जो देता है five point two three times ten to the minus three siemens per centimetre।

आख़िर में, molar conductivity बराबर kappa गुणा one thousand बटा molarity: five point two three times ten to the minus three, गुणा one thousand, बटा zero point zero five zero, जो आता है one hundred four point five siemens centimetre-squared per mole।
<whisper>उस thousand पर नज़र रखो।</whisper> One thousand से multiply करना भूल जाना इस तरह के सवाल में सबसे आम slip है।

segments.text: Two examples that reward reasoning. First, a NEET speed trap. A student dilutes a strong-electrolyte solution, potassium nitrate, to ten times its original volume. What happens to the conductivity and to the molar conductivity?

Do not compute; reason about the crowd. Diluting spreads the same ions through ten times the volume, so charge-carriers per cubic centimetre drop sharply and the conductivity decreases. But molar conductivity fixes the amount at one mole and only asks how freely the ions move, so with neighbours farther apart it increases modestly, toward the limiting value.
The trap is that because both terms contain the word conductivity, students reflexively move them in the same direction. Anchor the one-liner: dilute, and kappa drops while molar conductivity lifts.
Now a JEE Main example using Kohlrausch's law. Find the limiting molar conductivity of propanoic acid.

We are given three limiting molar conductivities: hydrochloric acid is four hundred twenty six, sodium propanoate is eighty six, and sodium chloride is one hundred twenty six, all in siemens centimetre-squared per mole.
Since propanoic acid is weak, we route through Kohlrausch, as the board shows: hydrochloric acid plus the sodium propanoate, minus sodium chloride.

That is four hundred twenty six plus eighty six minus one hundred twenty six, which equals three hundred eighty six siemens centimetre-squared per mole. Check: the sodium and chloride cancel, leaving the hydrogen ion and the propanoate ion, exactly the ions of propanoic acid.

दो examples जो reasoning को reward करते हैं। पहला, एक NEET speed trap। एक student एक strong-electrolyte solution, potassium nitrate, को उसके original volume का दस गुना dilute करता है। Conductivity और molar conductivity का क्या होता है?

Compute मत करो; भीड़ के हिसाब से सोचो। Dilution वही ions को दस गुना volume में फैला देता है, तो per cubic centimetre charge-carriers तेज़ी से गिरते हैं और conductivity घटती है। पर molar conductivity amount को one mole पर fix करती है और सिर्फ़ पूछती है कि ions कितनी आज़ादी से move करते हैं, तो पड़ोसी दूर होने पर वह modestly बढ़ती है, limiting value की ओर।
Trap यह है कि दोनों terms में conductivity शब्द होने से students उन्हें एक ही direction में ले जाते हैं। यह one-liner पकड़ो: dilute करो, तो kappa गिरता है जबकि molar conductivity चढ़ती है।
अब Kohlrausch's law इस्तेमाल करके एक JEE Main example। Propanoic acid की limiting molar conductivity निकालो।

हमें तीन limiting molar conductivities दी हैं: hydrochloric acid four hundred twenty six, sodium propanoate eighty six, और sodium chloride one hundred twenty six, सब siemens centimetre-squared per mole में।
चूँकि propanoic acid weak है, हम Kohlrausch से route करते हैं, जैसा board दिखाता है: hydrochloric acid plus sodium propanoate, minus sodium chloride।

यानी four hundred twenty six plus eighty six minus one hundred twenty six, जो बराबर three hundred eighty six siemens centimetre-squared per mole। Check: sodium और chloride cancel हो जाते हैं, बचते हैं hydrogen ion और propanoate ion, ठीक propanoic acid के ions।

board_events.text: Small $\alpha$ (~10%) confirms HA is genuinely weak, since $\Lambda_m \ll \Lambda^{\circ}_m$.

segments.text: Now a full JEE Advanced calculation tying it together. A zero point zero two zero molar solution of a monobasic weak acid has a conductivity of eight point zero times ten to the minus four siemens per centimetre. Its limiting molar conductivity is three hundred ninety siemens centimetre-squared per mole. Find the degree of dissociation and the dissociation constant.
So we have the concentration, the measured conductivity, and the limiting molar conductivity. The board walks the three steps.

Step one, the molar conductivity at this concentration. That is kappa times one thousand over the molarity: eight point zero times ten to the minus four, times one thousand, over zero point zero two zero, which is forty siemens centimetre-squared per mole.
Step two, the degree of dissociation. Alpha is the molar conductivity over the limiting value: forty over three hundred ninety, which is zero point one zero two six.

Step three, the dissociation constant, from Ostwald's dilution law. It is c alpha squared over one minus alpha: zero point zero two zero times zero point one zero two six squared, over zero point eight nine seven four.
Working that out gives about two point three five times ten to the minus four.

<chuckle>And a nice sanity check:</chuckle> the small alpha, only about ten percent, confirms the acid is genuinely weak, exactly consistent with its molar conductivity being far below the limiting value.

अब एक full JEE Advanced calculation जो सब कुछ जोड़ती है। एक monobasic weak acid के zero point zero two zero molar solution की conductivity है eight point zero times ten to the minus four siemens per centimetre। इसकी limiting molar conductivity है three hundred ninety siemens centimetre-squared per mole। Degree of dissociation और dissociation constant निकालो।
तो हमारे पास concentration, measured conductivity, और limiting molar conductivity हैं। Board तीन steps चलता है।

Step one, इस concentration पर molar conductivity। यानी kappa गुणा one thousand बटा molarity: eight point zero times ten to the minus four, गुणा one thousand, बटा zero point zero two zero, जो है forty siemens centimetre-squared per mole।
Step two, degree of dissociation। Alpha बराबर molar conductivity बटा limiting value: forty बटा three hundred ninety, यानी zero point one zero two six।

Step three, dissociation constant, Ostwald's dilution law से। यह बराबर c alpha squared बटा one minus alpha: zero point zero two zero गुणा zero point one zero two six का square, बटा zero point eight nine seven four।
इसे हल करने पर मिलता है करीब two point three five times ten to the minus four।
<chuckle>और एक अच्छा sanity check:</chuckle> छोटा alpha, सिर्फ़ करीब दस percent, confirm करता है कि acid सच में weak है, ठीक इसके molar conductivity के limiting value से बहुत नीचे होने के अनुरूप।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for conductance

board_events.text: Where marks quietly leak
$\kappa$ and $\Lambda_m$ oppose on dilution: $\kappa\downarrow$, $\Lambda_m\uparrow$.
Dropping or misplacing the 1000: only valid with $\kappa$ in S cm$^{-1}$ and mol L$^{-1}$.
Never apply $\alpha=\Lambda_m/\Lambda^{\circ}_m$ to a strong electrolyte; that formula is for weak ones.
In Kohlrausch, verify the spectator ions (Na+, Cl-) actually cancel.
Sanity check: typical $\Lambda_m$ is a few to a few hundred S cm$^{2}$ mol$^{-1}$.
An answer like $0.12$ or $12000$ almost always signals a 1000-factor slip.
For a weak acid, expect small $\alpha$ ($<0.2$); a large $\alpha$ means you inverted the ratio.

segments.text: Let's close with the traps that quietly leak marks in conductance problems.

First and biggest: kappa and molar conductivity oppose each other on dilution. Kappa goes down, molar conductivity goes up. Because both words contain conductivity, students move them together, and that is wrong.

Second, dropping or misplacing the factor of one thousand. The formula molar conductivity equals kappa times one thousand over molarity is only valid when kappa is in siemens per centimetre and concentration in moles per litre. Always write units beside every number.

Third, never apply the alpha equals molar-conductivity-over-limiting formula to a strong electrolyte. That formula is for weak electrolytes. A strong one is essentially fully dissociated already, and its gap below the limiting value comes from interionic forces, not incomplete dissociation.

Fourth, in Kohlrausch, always verify that the spectator ions actually cancel. Set it up as the acid equals hydrochloric acid plus the sodium salt minus sodium chloride, and check the sodium and chloride vanish.

<whisper>Now two quick sanity checks that catch most errors.</whisper> After any molar-conductivity calculation, expect an answer from a few up to a few hundred siemens centimetre-squared per mole for typical solutions.
So an answer like zero point one two, or twelve thousand, almost always signals a one-thousand-factor slip. Go back and check where the thousand went.

And for a weak acid, the degree of dissociation should come out small, below about zero point two at ordinary concentrations. A large alpha means you mislabelled the electrolyte or inverted the ratio.
Conductance problems में चुपचाप marks leak करने वाले traps के साथ close करते हैं।

पहला और सबसे बड़ा: kappa और molar conductivity dilution पर एक-दूसरे के उल्टे चलते हैं। Kappa नीचे, molar conductivity ऊपर। चूँकि दोनों शब्दों में conductivity है, students उन्हें साथ ले जाते हैं, और यह ग़लत है।

दूसरा, one thousand का factor छोड़ना या ग़लत जगह लगाना। Formula molar conductivity बराबर kappa गुणा one thousand बटा molarity सिर्फ़ तब valid है जब kappa siemens per centimetre में हो और concentration moles per litre में। हर number के आगे units लिखो।

तीसरा, alpha बराबर molar-conductivity-over-limiting वाला formula strong electrolyte पर कभी मत लगाओ। वह formula weak electrolytes के लिए है। Strong तो पहले से essentially fully dissociated होता है, और उसका limiting value से नीचे gap interionic forces से आता है, incomplete dissociation से नहीं।

चौथा, Kohlrausch में हमेशा verify करो कि spectator ions सच में cancel होते हैं। इसे acid बराबर hydrochloric acid plus sodium salt minus sodium chloride लगाओ, और check करो कि sodium और chloride ग़ायब हो जाएँ।

<whisper>अब दो quick sanity checks जो ज़्यादातर errors पकड़ लेते हैं।</whisper> किसी भी molar-conductivity calculation के बाद typical solutions के लिए answer कुछ से लेकर कुछ सौ siemens centimetre-squared per mole तक expect करो।
तो zero point one two, या twelve thousand जैसा answer लगभग हमेशा one-thousand-factor slip का संकेत है। वापस जाकर check करो कि thousand कहाँ गया।
और weak acid के लिए degree of dissociation छोटा आना चाहिए, ordinary concentrations पर करीब zero point two से नीचे। बड़ा alpha मतलब आपने electrolyte को ग़लत label किया या ratio उल्टा कर दिया।

board_events.text: The clearest bridge is the Daniell cell itself, run against an opposing voltage.
At exactly $1.1$ V the cell freezes; push past it and the reaction reverses.
Now Zn plates back on and Cu dissolves: the cell has become electrolytic.
Polarity flips: anode is $+$, cathode is $-$ (a battery drives it).

segments.text: In the last two subtopics a galvanic cell let a spontaneous reaction push electrons out and do work for us. An electrolytic cell runs the whole story in reverse: we force electrons in from an external battery to drive a reaction that would never happen on its own.
Think of the galvanic cell as water flowing downhill and turning a wheel. The electrolytic cell is a pump using external power to push that same water back up the hill.
Here is the setup: an external direct-current source wired to two inert electrodes in an electrolyte.
The clearest bridge between the two is the Daniell cell itself. Apply an opposing voltage and raise it slowly.
<curious>Watch what happens at the threshold.</curious> At exactly one point one volts the cell freezes, no current flows. Push past one point one volts and the reaction reverses.

Now zinc plates back on and copper dissolves. The cell has become electrolytic. That single experiment captures the whole idea: above the cell's own e m f, the external source wins and chemistry runs backward.
And crucially, the polarity flips. In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive and the cathode is negative, because a battery is driving it, exactly the opposite of a galvanic cell.

पिछले दो subtopics में एक galvanic cell ने एक spontaneous reaction को electrons बाहर push करके हमारे लिए काम करने दिया। एक electrolytic cell पूरी कहानी उल्टी चलाता है: हम एक external battery से electrons अंदर force करते हैं ताकि एक ऐसी reaction चले जो अपने आप कभी न होती।
Galvanic cell को पानी समझो जो नीचे बहकर एक wheel घुमाता है। Electrolytic cell एक pump है जो external power से उसी पानी को वापस ऊपर धकेलता है।
यह रहा setup: एक external direct-current source, दो inert electrodes से जुड़ा, एक electrolyte में।
दोनों के बीच सबसे साफ़ bridge है Daniell cell ख़ुद। एक opposing voltage लगाओ और धीरे-धीरे बढ़ाओ।
<curious>Threshold पर क्या होता है देखो।</curious> Exactly one point one volts पर cell जम जाता है, कोई current नहीं। One point one volts से आगे बढ़ाओ तो reaction उल्टी हो जाती है।
अब zinc वापस plate होता है और copper घुलता है। Cell electrolytic बन गया। वह एक experiment पूरा idea पकड़ लेता है: cell के अपने e m f से ऊपर, external source जीतता है और chemistry उल्टी चलती है।
और सबसे अहम, polarity flip हो जाती है। Electrolytic cell में anode positive और cathode negative, क्योंकि इसे एक battery चला रही है, galvanic cell से बिल्कुल उल्टा।

One Faraday = one mole of electrons = 96500 C = one equivalent.

board_events.caption: The price in electrons

board_events.text: The price in electrons is set by the charge on the ion: Ag $1F$, Cu $2F$, Al $3F$.

segments.text: Now for the accountant of this whole subtopic. Michael Faraday's great insight was that the amount of chemistry at an electrode is simply bookkeeping on electrons.

Pass a fixed number of electrons and you get a fixed amount of product, no more, no less. One mole of electrons is one Faraday, ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs, and it deposits exactly one equivalent of any substance.
The diagram shows the pricing. To get one mole of silver you spend one Faraday, because silver needs one electron. For one mole of copper you spend two Faraday, and for aluminium, three.
Start from the charge passed: charge equals current times time.

The first law says the mass liberated is proportional to that charge. In terms of molar mass and electrons per ion, the mass equals molar mass times current times time, all over n times the Faraday constant.
The second law compares two cells in series. For the same charge, the masses are in the ratio of their equivalent weights.
<whisper>Here is the whole trick in one line:</whisper> the price in electrons is set by the charge on the ion. Silver costs one Faraday per mole, copper two, aluminium three.
अब इस पूरे subtopic का accountant। Michael Faraday की महान insight यह थी कि electrode पर chemistry की मात्रा बस electrons की bookkeeping है।

एक निश्चित संख्या में electrons pass करो और एक निश्चित amount product मिलता है, न ज़्यादा न कम। One mole electrons बराबर one Faraday, ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs, और यह किसी भी पदार्थ का exactly one equivalent deposit करता है।
Diagram pricing दिखाता है। One mole silver पाने के लिए आप one Faraday ख़र्च करते हो, क्योंकि silver को one electron चाहिए। One mole copper के लिए two Faraday, और aluminium के लिए three।
Charge passed से शुरू करो: charge बराबर current गुणा time।
First law कहता है mass liberated उस charge के proportional है। Molar mass और electrons per ion के हिसाब से, mass बराबर molar mass गुणा current गुणा time, पूरे का n गुणा Faraday constant से भाग।
Second law series में दो cells की तुलना करता है। एक ही charge के लिए, masses उनके equivalent weights के ratio में होती हैं।
<whisper>पूरा trick एक line में:</whisper> electrons में क़ीमत ion के charge से तय होती है। Silver की क़ीमत one Faraday per mole, copper की two, aluminium की three।

board_events.text: Cathode: the species with the more positive reduction potential is favoured.
In aqueous NaCl, H+/H2 ($0.00$ V) beats Na+/Na ($-2.71$ V), so H2 is released.
Anode: the lower reduction potential is favoured, but check overpotential.
Water "should" oxidise, but O2 evolution is slow, so Cl2 comes off instead.
Molten NaCl has no water: products are simply Na and Cl2.

segments.text: There is a subtlety in aqueous solutions: water itself can react, and that changes what you get.
The diagram contrasts the two cases side by side, molten sodium chloride against the aqueous solution.
At the cathode, reduction, the species with the more positive reduction potential is favoured.

So in aqueous sodium chloride, you might expect sodium metal, but the hydrogen couple at zero volts beats the sodium couple at minus two point seven one volts. Water is reduced more easily, so hydrogen gas comes off, not sodium.
At the anode, oxidation, the species with the lower reduction potential is favoured, but here you must check overpotential.
By potentials alone, water should oxidise before chloride. But the oxygen reaction is kinetically sluggish and needs an extra push, an overpotential, so chlorine actually comes off instead.

Contrast that with molten sodium chloride, which has no water at all. There the products are simply sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. So products depend on who is present, their electrode potentials, and the kinetics.
Aqueous solutions में एक subtlety है: पानी ख़ुद react कर सकता है, और यह बदल देता है कि आपको क्या मिलता है।
Diagram दोनों cases साथ-साथ दिखाता है, molten sodium chloride बनाम aqueous solution।
Cathode पर, reduction, ज़्यादा positive reduction potential वाली species favoured होती है।

तो aqueous sodium chloride में आप sodium metal की उम्मीद कर सकते हो, पर hydrogen couple zero volts पर sodium couple minus two point seven one volts को हरा देता है। पानी ज़्यादा आसानी से reduce होता है, तो hydrogen gas निकलती है, sodium नहीं।
Anode पर, oxidation, कम reduction potential वाली species favoured होती है, पर यहाँ overpotential check करना ज़रूरी है।
सिर्फ़ potentials से, पानी को chloride से पहले oxidise होना चाहिए। पर oxygen reaction kinetically सुस्त है और एक extra push, यानी overpotential, माँगती है, तो chlorine बजाय निकलती है।

इसकी तुलना molten sodium chloride से करो, जिसमें पानी है ही नहीं। वहाँ products बस cathode पर sodium और anode पर chlorine। तो products इस पर depend करते हैं कि कौन मौजूद है, उनके electrode potentials, और kinetics।

board_events.text: Primary: used once, reactants run out (dry cell, mercury cell).
Secondary: rechargeable, reaction reversed by an external source (lead storage, Ni-Cd).
Lead storage: acid is consumed, so electrolyte density falls on discharge.
Fuel cells skip combustion, so they are far more efficient and near pollution-free.

segments.text: Batteries are just galvanic cells packaged to be portable. We sort them into three families, shown here.
The diagram lays them out: primary, secondary, and fuel cells.
Primary cells are used once: the reactants simply run out and cannot be replaced. The dry cell and the mercury cell are the examples to know.
Secondary cells are rechargeable: the reaction can be reversed by an external source. The lead storage battery and the nickel-cadmium cell are the classics.
Here is the lead-storage discharge reaction: lead plus lead dioxide plus sulphuric acid give lead sulphate plus water.
Notice that sulphuric acid is consumed and water is formed, so the electrolyte density falls on discharge, and charging reverses the whole reaction.

The third family is the fuel cell, where reactants are fed in continuously from outside, so it never runs down as long as fuel flows. The hydrogen-oxygen cell has just one overall reaction, hydrogen plus oxygen giving water.

<excited>And here is why engineers love them:</excited> a thermal power plant burns fuel, makes steam, and spins a turbine, wasting most energy as heat at around forty percent efficiency. A fuel cell skips combustion and the turbine entirely, converting chemical energy straight to electricity, so it is far more efficient and essentially pollution-free.
Batteries बस galvanic cells हैं जो portable बनाने के लिए package की गई हैं। हम उन्हें तीन families में बाँटते हैं, यहाँ दिखाई गईं।
Diagram उन्हें रखता है: primary, secondary, और fuel cells।
Primary cells एक बार इस्तेमाल होते हैं: reactants बस ख़त्म हो जाते हैं और replace नहीं हो सकते। Dry cell और mercury cell जानने लायक examples हैं।
Secondary cells rechargeable होते हैं: reaction को external source से उल्टा किया जा सकता है। Lead storage battery और nickel-cadmium cell classics हैं।
यह रही lead-storage discharge reaction: lead plus lead dioxide plus sulphuric acid देते हैं lead sulphate plus water।
ध्यान दो कि sulphuric acid consume होता है और water बनता है, तो electrolyte density discharge पर गिरती है, और charging पूरी reaction उल्टी कर देती है।
तीसरी family है fuel cell, जहाँ reactants बाहर से लगातार feed होते हैं, तो जब तक fuel बहता है यह कभी नहीं थकता। Hydrogen-oxygen cell की बस एक overall reaction है, hydrogen plus oxygen देते हैं water।

<excited>और यही वजह है कि engineers इन्हें पसंद करते हैं:</excited> एक thermal power plant fuel जलाता है, steam बनाता है, turbine घुमाता है, ज़्यादातर energy heat की तरह बर्बाद करते हुए करीब forty percent efficiency पर। Fuel cell combustion और turbine पूरी तरह skip कर देता है, chemical energy सीधे electricity में बदलते हुए, तो यह कहीं ज़्यादा efficient और essentially pollution-free है।
